questions.question_text: When must a Wyoming licensee make the written brokerage relationship disclosure to a prospective buyer?
questions.correct_answer: Before any discussion incidental to a sale or lease
distractors: At the time of the first written offer
Within 48 hours of the first showing
At closing or settlement
questions.explanation: The written relationship disclosure must be made before engaging in any discussion or arrangement incidental to a sale, purchase, exchange or lease, and before entering any written agreement (W.S. 33-28-306(a)). Open house showings, preliminary conversations and requests for factual information are expressly carved out, so casual property talk alone does not trigger it.

questions.question_text: A Wyoming licensee shows a home at an open house to a walk-in buyer and answers factual questions, but provides no relationship disclosure. What is the result?
questions.correct_answer: No violation; showings and factual questions are exempt
distractors: A violation, because any showing triggers disclosure
A violation, because the buyer became a client
A violation unless disclosure follows within 48 hours
questions.explanation: Open house showings, preliminary conversations and requests for factual information expressly do not constitute discussions or arrangements incidental to a sale (W.S. 33-28-306(a)), so no disclosure was due and no violation occurred. The walk-in is a customer, not a client; answering factual questions does not create an agency relationship.

questions.question_text: What must Wyoming's written relationship disclosure include regarding intermediary duties?
questions.correct_answer: A conspicuous statement of duties NOT owed
distractors: Only a list of duties the intermediary owes
A signature line for WREC approval
The intermediary's commission rate
questions.explanation: The disclosure must carry a conspicuous statement of the duties and obligations owed by an agent but NOT owed by an intermediary (W.S. 33-28-306(a)(iii)). An agent promotes the client's interests with utmost good faith, loyalty and fidelity; an intermediary owes no such fiduciary duties and is neither agent nor advocate for any party.

questions.question_text: A licensee provides agency disclosure after the buyer signs a buyer-broker agreement. Has the licensee complied?
questions.correct_answer: No, disclosure must precede any written agreement
distractors: Yes, the agreement itself serves as disclosure
Yes, if delivered within 24 hours after signing
No, but only a written warning is issued
questions.explanation: Wyoming requires that agency disclosure be provided before entering any written agreement. Providing disclosure after the buyer-broker agreement is signed violates the timing requirement, regardless of how quickly it was delivered afterward.

questions.question_text: Which relationship types must be described in Wyoming's agency disclosure form?
distractors: Agent and dual agent only
Buyer's agent and seller's agent only
Fiduciary and non-fiduciary only
questions.explanation: The written disclosure must describe all three relationship types recognized in Wyoming: agent, intermediary, and customer. By explaining each type and the corresponding duties, the consumer can make an informed choice about their level of representation.

questions.question_text: A Wyoming seller knows the basement floods every spring, but the listing licensee also knows. What does Wyoming law require?
questions.correct_answer: The licensee must disclose the known adverse material fact
distractors: The seller must complete a state property disclosure statement
The seller must file a disclaimer statement with WREC
Nothing; the buyer must discover it by inspection
questions.explanation: Wyoming has no statute requiring a residential seller to deliver a property disclosure statement; the state follows caveat emptor, and W.S. 34-1-151 reaches only vacant land with no habitable dwelling. The duty falls on the licensee: a seller's agent must disclose to any prospective buyer all adverse material facts actually known, including the property's physical condition (W.S. 33-28-303(c)).

questions.question_text: An estate executor is selling an inherited Wyoming home and has never visited it. What does Wyoming law require of the executor?
questions.correct_answer: No property disclosure; Wyoming has no seller mandate
distractors: A signed disclaimer statement before offer acceptance
A WREC property condition disclosure statement
A licensed inspector's report at the executor's expense
questions.explanation: Wyoming has no statute requiring a residential seller to deliver any property disclosure or disclaimer form; the state follows caveat emptor, and W.S. 34-1-151 reaches only vacant land with no habitable dwelling. An executor is separately exempt from the Real Estate Act unless the executor is a licensee. A seller still may not actively conceal a defect.

questions.question_text: Which statement accurately describes Wyoming's seller property disclosure law?
questions.correct_answer: Wyoming has no residential seller disclosure statute
distractors: Disclosures must be re-dated every 180 days
A disclaimer statement may substitute when the seller lacks knowledge
WREC prescribes a mandatory disclosure form for all sales
questions.explanation: Wyoming imposes no statutory residential seller property-disclosure requirement; it is a caveat emptor jurisdiction. The disclosure/disclaimer system with a 180-day dating rule comes from a 2001 bill, SF0158, that never became law; Title 34, chapter 26 is "Notarial Acts." The only Wyoming property-disclosure statute, W.S. 34-1-151, applies to vacant land only.

questions.question_text: When must a Wyoming responsible broker disclose in writing who is paying compensation in the transaction?
questions.correct_answer: Before the parties enter a contract to buy or sell
distractors: Within 10 days after mutual acceptance
At the final walkthrough before closing
At or before the closing date
questions.explanation: Before entering a written agreement with the seller and buyer, or before a contract to buy or sell, the responsible broker must disclose in writing to both parties the relationships of everyone paying the broker compensation (W.S. 33-28-308(f)). Written consent is separately required before a broker may be compensated by more than one party.

questions.question_text: A licensee suspects a property has mold but has no confirmed knowledge. Must the licensee inspect for mold?
questions.correct_answer: No, licensees are not required to inspect
distractors: Yes, all suspected hazards must be verified
Yes, under W.S. 33-28-303(d) duties
Only if the buyer requests it in writing
questions.explanation: Licensees must disclose adverse material facts actually known to them, but they owe no duty to conduct an independent inspection or to verify statements made by the seller or an inspector (W.S. 33-28-303(c), (d)). Suspicion without actual knowledge does not create an inspection duty.

questions.question_text: A Wyoming licensee wants to buy, for themselves, a home listed by another brokerage. What does Wyoming law require?
questions.correct_answer: Disclosure of their interest in the transaction
distractors: Nothing; the owner exemption applies to licensees
Their commission history disclosed to the seller
Written WREC approval before making the offer
questions.explanation: Wyoming has no standalone "licensed status disclosure" statute. What applies is the ground for discipline at W.S. 33-28-111(a)(iii), "failing to disclose an interest in the transaction." The owner/immediate-family exemption from the Act does not apply when that person is a licensee, so the licensee stays fully subject to the Act.

questions.question_text: A licensee's spouse wants to buy a property the licensee has listed. What disclosure is required?
questions.correct_answer: Disclose the personal interest in the transaction
distractors: No disclosure needed for a spouse's purchase
Only verbal notice to the other party
Transfer the listing to another brokerage
questions.explanation: "Failing to disclose an interest in the transaction" is a ground for discipline (W.S. 33-28-111(a)(iii)), and a spouse buying a property the licensee has listed is a personal interest that must be disclosed. An intermediary must separately disclose interests adverse to either party. Wyoming prescribes no particular form, though documenting the disclosure is prudent.

questions.question_text: A licensee sells an investment property they own to a client. The licensee does not disclose their ownership. What is the consequence?
questions.correct_answer: A conflict of interest disclosure violation
distractors: No issue if price is at fair market value
A minor paperwork deficiency at most
Permissible if the broker approves it
questions.explanation: A licensee must disclose their personal interest in any transaction, including ownership of property being sold. Failing to disclose this creates an undisclosed conflict of interest, which violates Wyoming law regardless of whether the price was fair.

questions.question_text: A Wyoming licensee leases a property they own to their sibling and discloses nothing about their ownership. Which requirement was violated?
questions.correct_answer: The duty to disclose an interest in the transaction
distractors: A written licensed-status disclosure requirement
The 180-day disclaimer statement rule
No disclosure rules apply to lease transactions
questions.explanation: "Failing to disclose an interest in the transaction" is a ground for discipline, and the owner/immediate-family exemption from the Real Estate Act does not apply when the owner is a licensee (W.S. 33-28-111(a)(iii), 33-28-103(a)(i)). Wyoming has no separate written "licensed status" disclosure rule; that is other states' law. The relationship-disclosure statute covers leases as well as sales.

questions.question_text: Which of the following triggers a Wyoming licensee's duty to disclose an interest in the transaction?
questions.correct_answer: A licensee buying a listed property for personal use
distractors: Listing a property for a client
Showing a rental to a prospective tenant
Attending an open house as a visitor
questions.explanation: "Failing to disclose an interest in the transaction" is a ground for discipline (W.S. 33-28-111(a)(iii)). Buying a property for one's own account is a personal interest that must be disclosed, while routine professional activity such as listing for a client, showing a rental, or attending an open house creates none. Wyoming has no separate "licensed status" disclosure statute.
